common_name: Rhea Dwarf Mealy Blue Sage (Compact Bedding Salvia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost or set out transplants after frost danger passes, in well-drained garden soil in full sun; Rhea's dwarf, uniform habit makes it a reliable front-of-border or mass bedding choice.

directions: Rhea is a dwarf selection of mealy blue sage, holding to a tidy 12-18 inches tall versus the 2-3 feet typical of the species, which makes it useful where taller cultivars like Victoria Blue would flop or overwhelm a bed edge. Dense spikes of dark violet-blue flowers rise continuously over narrow gray-green foliage from late spring through frost, drawing bees and occasional hummingbird visits without the need for deadheading. It tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, performing reliably as a summer annual across most of the country and as a short-lived perennial in zone 8-10 gardens. Its compact, uniform habit and darker flower color make it a popular choice for mass plantings and container edges where the taller, looser 'Victoria Blue' would be out of scale.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full to part sun; Amante is a guaranitica x gesneriiflora hybrid that needs a full growing season to reach its mature size.

directions: Amante is a hybrid between Salvia guaranitica (a 'Black and Blue' parent) and Salvia gesneriiflora, combining the near-black stems and calyces of both parents with hot fuchsia-red flowers rather than the usual guaranitica blue. It blooms from early summer straight through frost on a vigorous, upright plant that quickly reaches 4-5 feet, so give it room at the back of a border. Hummingbirds treat it as a favorite nectar source, often preferring the intense pink-red color over neighboring blue salvias. In zone 8-9 it usually dies back to the roots in winter and resprouts from the crown in spring; further south it stays evergreen and shrubby, and everywhere it benefits from a hard cutback in late winter to keep growth dense rather than leggy.

common_name: Windwalker Royal Red Salvia (Cold-Hardy Hummingbird Sage)

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; a Plant Select introduction bred from Salvia darcyi x microphylla 'Raspberry Delight', it is markedly more cold-hardy than either parent species alone.

directions: Bred by Colorado nurseryman Kelly Grummons by crossing the tender Mexican species Salvia darcyi with the hardier Salvia microphylla 'Raspberry Delight', Windwalker Royal Red combines vivid blood-red, tubular flowers with reliable perennial hardiness well north of where most red Mexican sages survive winter. Robust upright stems bloom continuously from late June into October and are worked heavily by hummingbirds, visible from a distance thanks to the saturated red color. It forms a sturdy 3-4 foot mound and performs best in hot, sunny, rocky or sandy sites with minimal supplemental irrigation; overly rich or consistently moist soil produces a looser, floppier plant. Cut the woody framework back hard in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Phyllis' Fancy Sage (Long-Spiked Lavender Bicolor Salvia)

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this chance seedling from the UC Santa Cruz Arboretum forms a large mounding shrub and needs several seasons to reach mature size.

directions: Phyllis' Fancy is a chance seedling discovered at the University of California Santa Cruz Arboretum, believed to be a cross involving Salvia leucantha, and named for horticulturist Phyllis Norris. From midsummer to frost it produces foot-long spikes carrying soft lavender-white flowers nestled in dark blue-purple bracts, giving a two-tone effect that persists even after individual blooms fade. The plant grows into a large, evergreen, mounding shrub 4-5 feet tall and wide, considerably bigger than most Mexican bush sage cultivars, so it needs generous room at the back of a border. It draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds over an unusually long season and, like other velvet sages, tolerates heat and drought well once established but benefits from a hard cutback where winters dip into the mid-20s.

common_name: Whirly Blue Cleveland Sage (Large-Flowered California Native Hybrid)

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall or spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; a natural hybrid of Salvia clevelandii and S. leucophylla, it needs excellent drainage and should not be irrigated through summer once established.

directions: Whirly Blue is a hybrid between two California native sages, Salvia clevelandii and S. leucophylla, combining the intensely fragrant gray-green foliage of both parents with unusually large whorls of deep blue-lavender flowers on tall stalks held above the foliage. It blooms heaviest in late spring and summer, drawing bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies, and the aromatic leaves resist deer browsing. The shrub grows fast into a dense, wide mound 4-5 feet tall and often wider, so give it plenty of open ground rather than crowding it in a mixed border. Like other Cleveland sage selections it is adapted to summer-dry conditions and can suffer root rot with regular irrigation once established, making it best suited to a xeric or Mediterranean-style planting on the Gulf Coast's better-drained soils.

common_name: Hot Trumpets Cedar Sage (Compact Texas Native Red Salvia)

planting.note: Sow indoors or set out divisions/transplants around the last frost into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; cedar sage is a woodland-edge native of Texas limestone outcrops and appreciates protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Hot Trumpets is a selection of Texas native cedar sage prized for producing an especially heavy show of bright crimson-red, tubular flowers on compact 12-inch spikes in late spring and early summer, low enough that low-flying hummingbirds and long-tongued bees visit easily. The rounded, scalloped leaves form a neat low mound that suits woodland-edge and dappled-shade plantings beneath oaks, unlike most red-flowered salvias which demand full sun. It is native to limestone soils in the Texas Hill Country and adjacent Mexico, so it thrives in alkaline, well-drained sites and tolerates summer dry spells once established, going semi-dormant in the heat of late summer before returning with fall rains. Its diminutive size makes it a good choice for rock gardens, shaded borders, or naturalizing under mature trees where taller salvias would be out of scale.
